notes: Contextualised sequencing using the same audited step dependency graph; round levels range from foundation to extend. These are original teaching scenarios, not past-paper questions.

scenarios.title: Library repair check
scenarios.context: A school library has 240 eligible books in its repair register. The librarian wants to inspect 24 distinct books without choosing favourites.
scenarios.task: Construct a simple random sample of 24 books from the 240 eligible books.

steps.text: Create a complete register of the 240 eligible library books.
Assign each of the 240 books a different label from 1 to 240.
Generate unbiased random integers in the inclusive range 1 to 240.
Discard repeated book labels until there are exactly 24 different numbers.
Inspect the 24 books corresponding to the accepted random labels.

scenarios.workedExample: The random number generator supplies integers from 1 to 240. If label 68 appears twice, ignore its second appearance; draw until 24 different labels identify 24 books.
scenarios.caution: An incomplete register would leave eligible books with no selection chance. A correctly bounded generator produces no out-of-range values.

scenarios.title: Solar-panel inspection
scenarios.context: A technician maintains 1,200 solar modules on a large site. Exactly 75 different modules must undergo an inspection, with no preference for the nearest modules.
scenarios.task: Design a fair chance-based draw for 75 of the 1,200 modules.

steps.text: Prepare a complete list of all 1,200 modules eligible for inspection.
Number each module uniquely from 1 to 1,200 on the inspection list.
Use a uniform integer generator that returns labels between 1 and 1,200.
Ignore any repeated module number until 75 distinct labels have been drawn.
Visit and inspect the 75 modules matching the accepted number labels.

scenarios.workedExample: Use a generator bounded by 1 and 1,200; if number 901 is drawn twice, only its first occurrence counts towards the 75 different modules.
scenarios.caution: Random selection is impartial, but inaccessible or missing modules can cause nonresponse or incomplete coverage; do not replace them by convenience.

scenarios.title: Tree disease survey
scenarios.context: A park has 840 eligible trees mapped by identifier. Researchers want to assess disease prevalence using 70 different trees selected by chance.
scenarios.task: Set out a defensible simple random sample of 70 mapped trees.

steps.text: Check the register contains all 840 eligible trees in the target park.
Give the 840 eligible trees unique identifiers numbered 1 to 840.
Draw uniformly random whole-number labels between 1 and 840 inclusive.
Reject repeated tree identifiers until 70 different labels have been drawn.
Measure the 70 trees whose labels were retained from the random draw.

scenarios.workedExample: A selection could begin 12, 407, 12, 799: the second 12 is ignored, leaving three distinct trees so far; continue until there are 70.
scenarios.caution: Check recently planted trees are included in the frame. Equal chances for samples drawn from an incomplete frame do not fix undercoverage.

scenarios.title: Bottling-line quality check
scenarios.context: A quality-control officer has 480 bottles in a single production sequence and needs to inspect 40 at regular positions. Each bottle has a position in the ordered list.
scenarios.task: Construct a systematic sample of exactly 40 bottles.

steps.text: Number all 480 eligible bottles in the production order.
Calculate the fixed interval k = 480 / 40 = 12 bottles.
Randomly choose the first bottle position from 1 to 12.
Inspect that bottle and then every twelfth position until 40 are selected.

scenarios.workedExample: If the random start is 7, inspect positions 7, 19, 31, ... , 475, giving 40 different positions.
scenarios.caution: A repeating 12-bottle production pattern could distort the result. Consider whether ordered positions have relevant periodicity.

scenarios.title: Bus ticket records
scenarios.context: A transport office has 900 bus ticket records ordered by transaction time and requires 60 records for a systematic audit.
scenarios.task: Build a random-start systematic sample of 60 of the 900 records.

steps.text: Put all 900 eligible ticket records in a numbered time-ordered list.
Calculate the interval k = 900 / 60 = 15 records.
Choose one random starting record from positions 1 to 15.
Take the starting record, then every fifteenth one until 60 records are chosen.

scenarios.workedExample: With random start 9, the audit records are 9, 24, 39, ... , 894, exactly 60 positions.
scenarios.caution: Patterns linked to shifts or departures might repeat in the ordered records. Do not substitute 'start at 1' for a random start.

scenarios.title: Factory shift cycle
scenarios.context: A factory orders 720 production entries by time and plans to inspect 60 systematically. The entries may repeat the same type of workstation every 12 positions.
scenarios.task: Explain the systematic-selection sequence while remaining alert to periodic bias.

steps.text: Make an ordered numbered frame containing all 720 eligible production entries.
Calculate the exact interval k = 720 / 60 = 12 positions.
Randomly select one starting entry between positions 1 and 12.
Follow the start with entries 12 positions apart until 60 are included.

scenarios.workedExample: Starting at position 4 gives positions 4, 16, 28, ... , 712, which is a valid 60-position systematic selection.
scenarios.caution: Although mathematically systematic, this plan risks sampling the same workstation category repeatedly if the list has a 12-position cycle.

scenarios.title: Two-year-group survey
scenarios.context: A school has 240 Year 12 and 160 Year 13 students. Researchers need a proportional sample of 40 that gives both groups their planned share.
scenarios.task: Build proportional stratified random sampling for 40 of the 400 students.

steps.text: Separate the 400 eligible students into disjoint Year 12 and Year 13 registers.
Allocate (240 / 400) × 40 = 24 Year 12 places and (160 / 400) × 40 = 16 Year 13 places.
Randomly draw 24 distinct Year 12 students and 16 distinct Year 13 students from their own registers.
Combine both random draws into one 40-student sample.

scenarios.workedExample: Year 12 contributes 24 and Year 13 contributes 16: both counts are fixed before random selection inside the groups.
scenarios.caution: Matching year-group proportions does not by itself guarantee a representative sample for unrelated characteristics such as travel habits.

scenarios.title: Journey-to-school survey
scenarios.context: A school records each pupil's main travel mode: 180 bus users, 120 walkers and 100 car users. It wants a proportional random sample of 80.
scenarios.task: Work out and sequence the group-specific random sampling needed.

steps.text: Divide all 400 students into non-overlapping bus, walking and car groups using their main travel mode.
Randomly select 36 different bus users, 24 walkers and 20 car users from separate group lists.
Merge the three selected groups to form a sample of exactly 80 pupils.

scenarios.workedExample: The planned stratum counts are 36, 24 and 20, summing to 80; each group needs its own impartial random draw.
scenarios.caution: Specify one primary travel mode per student to avoid overlapping strata. Quotas alone, without random draws, would be a different method.

scenarios.title: Habitat biodiversity survey
scenarios.context: Environmental researchers classify 700 eligible plots: 330 coastal, 220 woodland and 150 wetland. They need a proportional sample of 60 whole plots.
scenarios.task: Plan an accurate proportional allocation and random draw within every habitat.

steps.text: Partition the 700 plots into mutually exclusive coastal, woodland and wetland lists.
Independently randomise and select 28 distinct coastal, 19 woodland and 13 wetland plots.
Combine the three random plot sets into one 60-plot sample.

scenarios.workedExample: The whole-number allocations 28, 19 and 13 sum to 60 and closely match the original proportions. Random selection within each stratum is compulsory.
scenarios.caution: Rounding must still leave exactly 60 plots. Do not choose accessible plots instead of random ones within each habitat.

scenarios.title: Science festival feedback
scenarios.context: A science festival wants feedback from 50 eligible attendees: 30 pupils and 20 adults. Interviewers will recruit willing people until those group targets are reached.
scenarios.task: Arrange a quota sampling procedure for the 50 responses.

steps.text: Define two non-overlapping eligible attendee groups: pupils and adults.
Set the desired response quotas at 30 pupils and 20 adults.
Approach willing festival visitors without a random draw and register each response in the right group.
Stop recruiting each group at its quota; finish with 30 pupil and 20 adult responses.

scenarios.workedExample: The interviewer may speak to the next willing visitors, provided the completed 50 responses meet the two targets. No random list is used.
scenarios.caution: Group counts alone do not make this stratified random sampling. Willing visitors can differ from people who refuse.

scenarios.title: Gym membership opinions
scenarios.context: A gym would like 40 volunteer responses: 24 from monthly members and 16 from annual members, recruited at its reception.
scenarios.task: Complete the quota approach while maintaining the agreed 24:16 split.

steps.text: Create clear monthly and annual membership groups without overlapping categories.
Set targets of 24 monthly-member and 16 annual-member completed responses.
Ask available consenting eligible members at reception without randomly selecting names.
Close each membership quota when full and stop after all 40 responses are obtained.

scenarios.workedExample: A receptionist can recruit members as they arrive; recruitment is non-random but the agreed group totals are controlled.
scenarios.caution: People who visit at different times may not be represented and the interviewer may overlook refusals.

scenarios.title: City transport priorities
scenarios.context: A city team wants 80 travel opinions by primary journey purpose: 35 school, 25 work and 20 leisure. Interviewers recruit available willing travellers.
scenarios.task: Plan a non-random quota procedure with three distinct group targets.

steps.text: Classify eligible travellers by one primary journey purpose: school, work or leisure.
Set separate completed-response quotas of 35 school, 25 work and 20 leisure journeys.
Recruit available eligible travellers non-randomly, recording each under exactly one journey-purpose category.
Stop each category at its set target and end the survey at 80 complete responses.

scenarios.workedExample: Collect 35+25+20=80 responses from accessible travellers. No random selection occurs within the three categories.
scenarios.caution: Because recruitment is non-random, matching the chosen purpose proportions does not establish population-wide representativeness.

scenarios.title: Gym entrance survey
scenarios.context: An investigator stands near a gym entrance at 5 pm and wants responses from 20 available members. No population register or subgroup quota is prepared.
scenarios.task: Put the eligible-volunteer opportunity sampling steps in a workable order.

steps.text: Specify that respondents must be current gym members able to consent.
Approach gym members who happen to be available at the entrance at 5 pm.
Collect responses from 20 willing eligible members and stop when the target is met.

scenarios.workedExample: The first 20 willing eligible members available at the chosen entrance can be surveyed directly.
scenarios.caution: The resulting group may differ from morning members and people who do not attend the gym that day.

scenarios.title: School tablet-use opinions
scenarios.context: A student researcher wants opinions from 35 Year 12 pupils found in the school canteen during lunch. There is no group target or random draw.
scenarios.task: Sequence an opportunity sample of eligible lunch-time volunteers.

steps.text: Define eligibility as pupils currently in Year 12 at the school.
Approach Year 12 pupils conveniently available in the canteen at lunchtime.
Ask willing eligible pupils about tablet use until 35 responses are collected.

scenarios.workedExample: The survey is quick because the researcher uses nearby eligible students, not a randomly selected school register.
scenarios.caution: Year 12 pupils absent from the canteen cannot enter this sample and might have different tablet-use habits.

scenarios.title: Waterfront litter survey
scenarios.context: At a waterfront event on Saturday morning, a researcher seeks 24 opinions about local litter by approaching available adult volunteers.
scenarios.task: Construct the practical opportunity-selection sequence without implying it is representative.

steps.text: Check respondents are adults eligible to give opinions on local waterfront litter.
Approach adult volunteers conveniently present at the Saturday waterfront event.
Record replies from 24 willing eligible adults, without random draws or quotas.

scenarios.workedExample: This recruitment strategy gives 24 convenient adult opinions but cannot be assumed to estimate views of all residents accurately.
scenarios.caution: People absent on Saturday morning and those not attending the event have little or no chance to respond.
